paper.title: "How Good Is EPSS, Really? A Five-Year Empirical Evaluation Correcting for Look-Ahead Bias"
paper.abstract: "Retrospective evaluations of the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) routinely apply current-day scores to historical Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records, creating a temporal information leak that inflates apparent performance. This paper presents the first multi-year empirical evaluation correcting for this look-ahead bias by using time-matched historical EPSS scores retrieved 30 days after each CVE publication date. Covering 134,821 fully-observed CVEs from 2021 to 2025 across five annual cohorts, with exploitation status determined from the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog under a fixed 12-month observation window, the study finds that: (1) using current-day scores inflates the prioritisation queue by 2.3x to 53.2x and collapses efficiency from 60.9% to 11.1% for the 2023 cohort; (2) EPSS Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) improves from 0.49 in 2021 to 0.92 in 2024 when evaluated with time-matched scores, while a CVSS-only baseline remains flat between 0.04 and 0.07; and (3) EPSS-elevated CVEs appear in Nuclei, proof-of-concept, and Metasploit exploit databases at 15x to 108x the cohort base rate. A fixed observation window methodology is introduced that makes cross-cohort exploitation rate comparisons valid. These results establish look-ahead bias as a first-order methodological error in EPSS evaluation and document EPSS as a substantially improving production ML system when assessed correctly."
